cells.tense: Right now the proportions between you and the people near you are being kept level, and it costs you nothing to hold.
cells.act: let the thing end that is already over
cells.ask: Stop feeding one arrangement with someone that already ran its course — no announcement, no last word. Let it be done.
cells.core:
You can feel what a fair exchange is without doing sums, and the passing back and forth with the people in your life moves. When something tips, you sense where to ease it back rather than auditing who owes what. The scale doesn't need watching because you're standing on it.

What this balance is free to feed next is an ending. There is something between you and another person that reached its finish some time ago and stays open out of habit — a standing arrangement, an old account neither of you closed. Endings that are actually finished don't need to be loud. Close one, quietly, and notice the room it leaves behind. Something new fills it sooner than you'd expect.
cells.sheetLine: The balance holds because you stop carrying what's finished.
cells.verb: To recalibrate what people owe each other until the proportions come right again
cells.place: Where a running balance between people is kept level without any still point

cells.tense: By the time the next exchange happens you will already have worked out what it's going to cost you.
cells.act: carry it without tightening around it
cells.ask: The next time you catch yourself tallying what someone owes, carry the whole account another hour without adding to the count or collecting on it.
cells.core:
Where you keep things level between people, something has sped up: exchanges get weighed before they happen, and who owes what gets tracked as though the running total were the relationship. Fairness like that has stopped being a sense and become an audit — you brace for the next transaction instead of letting one occur. Nobody's being cheated. It just costs more than the balance is worth.

What holds without crushing is carrying the whole account without closing your hand around it. Endurance is a body bearing weight, not a fist gripping it. You can hold what's owed you and still leave the ledger alone. Take one entry — something you're owed, something you owe — and carry it an hour without collecting or paying. Keep the shape you already have. When you set it down the amount hasn't changed; your grip has.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping score on exchanges that haven't happened yet.

cells.tense: For a long while now, things have been out of proportion around you and you have not been the one to say so.
cells.act: refine one piece by repeating it
cells.ask: Run something you can already do again this evening, alone and slowly — repetition for its own sake, not to fix anything and not to prove anything.
cells.core:
Where you are owed, you've been letting it stand. Things tip, and you absorb the tip rather than naming it; what's yours by right goes unclaimed and you carry the difference. That works for a while, then the room starts to feel like it's running on something you don't have. You can see the imbalance. Seeing it is not the part that's missing.

What restores the sense of proportion is repetition, done plain. A skill you already have, run again today, alone, with nobody watching and nothing riding on it — that is how fair dealing gets rebuilt, and it does not go through an argument. The session may feel pointless. Run it anyway. It comes back the way any skill does: small repeats, until you notice yourself asking for what you're owed without bracing first.
cells.sheetLine: You can see what isn't fair and you've stopped saying so.

cells.tense: The tally runs in you now without your hand on it — small debits, kept current, in a book you never opened.
cells.act: notice what you already know before you reason about it
cells.ask: When something between you and someone feels off, take your first read of it before you work out why — don't argue that read down afterward.
cells.core:
You keep the proportions level between the people close to you — easing one side, holding the other — and if asked you'd say it's not your doing. The tally is current. Somewhere in you a running count is kept, small withdrawals and deposits, and the story you tell has no bookkeeper in it. The count is felt by the people it's about, even when you can't see your own hand in it.

No argument is needed for what arrives before any reasoning does. Before you work out why something between you feels off, take the first read you had of it and give it room — it tends to be accurate, and it usually comes earlier than the explanation. Give the reasons their turn afterward. Naming that first read to yourself is the whole act; nobody else has to hear it for the count to come back into your hands.
cells.sheetLine: You keep a tally between people you don't know you're keeping.
cells.verb: To recalibrate what people owe each other until the proportions come right again
cells.place: Where a running balance between people is kept level without any still point

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the Too Little person's history made fairness feel dangerous — the record says only that the capacity is standing down, so the core must say where they stand (letting things go uncorrected) and nothing about what happened or what it cost. The reader could reasonably say they do push back hard when wronged, so every cell leaves room for 'no, that's not what's happening' and still hands them something usable. The asks survive being wrong: each is one small act of the medicine (Transformation's close-it, Fortitude's carry-it, Discipline's repeat-it, Wisdom's notice-what-you-know) that teaches something about the person's own capacity regardless of the read. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line about 'what is really underneath' the tallying — cut; the Unacknowledged cell describes the weighing happening in the open, not its cause.
